entries.explanation: Pong makes anticipation visible through a ball, a paddle and the space between them. Move this original paddle study to discover how the point of contact changes the next return.
entries.title: The angle of return

entries.explanation: Breakout turns each removed brick into a change in the ball's possible route. Steer this original paddle exercise and watch how a small opening can change the rhythm of an entire rally.
entries.title: A wall becomes a route

entries.explanation: Space Invaders organises pressure through an approaching formation and the timing of a shot. Move and fire in this original pattern study. A passing mothership offers a bonus above the formation: aiming for it means briefly leaving the nearer threat unattended.
entries.title: Reading a moving pattern

entries.explanation: Pac-Man gives a junction meaning by placing routes, pursuit and a goal in the same small space. Queue turns while movement continues in this original looping board. Clear the dots, read three different pursuers and decide when a power light or temporary fruit is worth a detour.
entries.title: Decisions at the junction

entries.explanation: Tetris makes the shape of an empty space as important as the shape falling towards it. Move and rotate pieces in this original packing study, using the landing guide to compare a quick fit with a decision that leaves room for the next piece.
entries.title: Read the space before it fills

entries.explanation: Spacewar! makes inertia and a central gravitational pull part of steering a spacecraft. Turn, thrust and brake in this original navigation study to compare the direction you face with the route your movement actually follows.
entries.title: Steering a continuing motion

entries.explanation: Elite uses wireframe edges to make a three-dimensional world readable without painted surfaces. Follow 120 approaching openings in this original depth study: their growing edges pass around your flight line, while a quiet pointer identifies the next opening. Small corrections made early are easier than a late turn. Hold the controller still briefly, then tilt to steer; the stick remains available. The route waits while the controller finds its neutral pose.
entries.title: Drawing a place with edges

entries.explanation: A platform game's jump is a designed curve, not just an upward movement. Follow an original route of rising platforms, choose between safe landings and optional high lights, and use flags to keep your progress. Hold or release the jump to change its arc. Run for extra speed, clear the pipes and catch the final flag high for a larger score.
entries.title: The shape of a jump

entries.explanation: Sonic the Hedgehog makes acceleration and momentum part of reading a route. Build speed on an original rolling landscape, carry momentum through a full loop and a low curved tunnel, jump its gaps or take the higher ledges. Braking deliberately sheds speed. At rest, combine braking with repeated jumps to charge a rolling start; release the brake to spend that stored motion. The checkpoint banks your rings, so a risky route has something to lose.
entries.title: Speed has a memory

entries.explanation: Celeste turns a jump and one short air dash into a sequence of commitments. Cross five original platforming rooms: clear a gap, touch a floating diamond to restore the dash in midair, then climb between safe ledges. Landing restores the dash too. A dotted arrow shows the direction you are aiming; the small diamond shows when another dash is available. Each lit doorway saves the next room, so a fall only repeats the current challenge.
entries.title: One clear burst

entries.explanation: Dance Dance Revolution connects a repeated beat to a precise window for action. Tap through this original rhythm study to hear and see the difference between matching a pulse and reacting after it.
entries.title: A moment inside the beat

entries.explanation: Lumines makes a musical scanline decide when a matching visual pattern clears. Arrange two-by-two colour groups in this original grid study and listen to how a timed sweep joins a spatial choice to a musical event.
entries.title: Build the pattern you hear

entries.explanation: Wolfenstein 3D constructs a first-person view by measuring distances across a map. Find three survey marks in an original corridor map and compare the plan with the wall heights that make it appear deep. The same space is read from above and at eye level.
entries.title: Distance becomes a wall

entries.explanation: Katamari Damacy makes a growing body change the meaning of the same surroundings. Roll and gather smaller objects in this original scale study to see an object that first resists collection become something you can gather.
entries.title: The room changes when you grow

entries.explanation: Portal makes momentum part of a spatial puzzle. Connect marked surfaces in five original chambers: cross a wall, turn a fall into distance, carry a cube onto an upper pressure plate, then solve a higher fling and a reversed launch. Speed survives each crossing while its direction follows the portal. A dotted arc previews the route your current movement will take. Choose surfaces with the right stick or touchpad; carry and release the cube close to it. The plate stays active only while it supports the cube.
entries.title: A fall becomes a way forward

entries.explanation: Gunpei Yokoi's approach to portable play makes constraints part of the design. Balance shades, motion, light and sound in an original prototype, then test three different briefs. The costs are illustrative design units, not measurements of historical hardware. The touchpad lets a design change beneath your finger.
entries.title: What does a pocket need?

entries.explanation: Koji Kondo treats music as part of how a game communicates action. Guide an original figure along a route and listen as rest, walking and running change the density of an original D-minor phrase. Its clock keeps moving instead of restarting at each change. Collect twelve lights and reach the flag.
entries.title: Let movement change the phrase

entries.explanation: Shigeru Miyamoto's platform games invite close attention to how a character moves. Tune gravity, lift and air control in this original jump laboratory, reach three flags and compare the pale trace of a previous landing with your next attempt. A short tap and a held jump produce different arcs.
entries.title: Keep the landing. Change the curve.

entries.explanation: SimCity invites a player to think in connected systems. In this original workshop, draw roads between homes, workplaces and a clinic, keep green space nearby, and follow the travelling dots. Change a route to see how journey length and congestion affect three construction briefs. These budgets and rules are illustrative, rather than a simulation of a real city.
entries.title: A city is a system

entries.explanation: Game Boy artwork builds a legible image from a small grid and four shades. Edit this original eight-by-eight drawing to see how changing one square can suggest an edge, a curve or the space between them.
entries.title: A picture, one pixel at a time

scope: Original interpretive studies of game design, art direction and music. Experiences open directly in fullscreen from their explanatory exhibit cards; controller glyphs appear along the bottom during play.
